from: South Carolina generally allows the named insured, their spouse, and resident relatives (so-called "class one" insureds) to stack across vehicles and policies, while a passenger or permissive driver ("class two") is usually limited to the coverage on the vehicle they were in. The rules also turn on which vehicles and policies were involved in the crash, which is exactly why every potentially applicable policy needs to be reviewed.
to: South Carolina permits certain insureds to stack UM/UIM coverage. Generally, a Class I insured (such as the named insured, spouse, or resident relative) may stack available coverage when an insured vehicle is involved, subject to S.C. Code § 38-77-160, including the limit based on the coverage carried on the vehicle involved in the accident. If none of the insured’s vehicles is involved, coverage is generally limited to the coverage available on one vehicle and stacking is not permitted. A passenger or permissive driver ("class two") is usually limited to the coverage on the vehicle they were in. Because the answer turns on which vehicles and policies were involved in the crash, every potentially applicable policy needs to be reviewed.
note: Approved wording, verbatim. NC-G3 resolved, approved 2026-09-30 (Gillin): stacking only for certain insureds, subject to § 38-77-160 incl. the vehicle-involved limit; no stacking when none of the insured's vehicles is involved.

from: Suppose an uninsured driver causes a crash that leaves you with $200,000 in damages, and you carry $100,000 in UM coverage on each of two household vehicles. Without stacking, you might be limited to a single $100,000 limit. With stacking, you may be able to combine them toward your $200,000 in losses.
to: Suppose an uninsured driver causes a crash that leaves you with $200,000 in damages while you are driving one of your two household vehicles, and you carry $100,000 in UM coverage on each. Without stacking, you might be limited to a single $100,000 limit. As a Class I insured with an insured vehicle involved, you may be able to stack the coverage on the other vehicle toward your $200,000 in losses, subject to the limit in S.C. Code § 38-77-160 based on the coverage on the vehicle involved. If neither vehicle had been involved in the crash, coverage would generally be limited to the coverage available on one vehicle, and stacking would not be permitted.

note: Key takeaways (ES). MC-G1 / B3-G4 resolved, approved 2026-09-30 (Gillin): cut comparative-fault helmet lines to the statute-only wording.

from: South Carolina requires helmets only for riders under age 21. However, like Georgia, not wearing a helmet can be raised as a comparative fault argument in your case.
to: South Carolina law requires motorcycle operators and passengers under age 21 to wear an approved helmet (S.C. Code § 56-5-3660). State law does not impose that helmet requirement on riders age 21 or older.
note: MC-G1 / B3-G4 resolved, approved 2026-09-30 (Gillin): cut comparative-fault helmet lines to the statute-only wording.

from: In either state, the defense may argue that not wearing a helmet contributed to your injuries, which could reduce your compensation under comparative fault rules.
to: In Georgia, the defense may argue that not wearing a helmet contributed to your injuries, which could reduce your compensation under comparative fault rules. South Carolina law does not impose a helmet requirement on riders age 21 or older (S.C. Code § 56-5-3660).
note: FAQ + FAQPage. The Georgia clause is kept as published; only the SC reach is removed. MC-G1 / B3-G4 resolved, approved 2026-09-30 (Gillin): cut comparative-fault helmet lines to the statute-only wording.

from: (In South Carolina, there is no universal helmet law for riders 21 and older — but the insurer may use lack of helmet to argue contributory negligence for head injuries)
to: (In South Carolina, the helmet requirement covers only motorcycle operators and passengers under 21 (S.C. Code § 56-5-3660); state law does not impose it on riders 21 or older)
note: "Contributory negligence" is also the wrong doctrine. MC-G1 / B3-G4 resolved, approved 2026-09-30 (Gillin): cut comparative-fault helmet lines to the statute-only wording.

from: Riders 21 and older may ride without helmets, but insurers may argue that failing to wear one contributed to head injury severity.
to: State law does not impose that helmet requirement on riders age 21 or older.
note: MC-G1 / B3-G4 resolved, approved 2026-09-30 (Gillin): cut comparative-fault helmet lines to the statute-only wording.

from: It can. South Carolina uses modified comparative negligence, so insurers may argue that not wearing a helmet increased your injuries and try to shift fault to you. Your award is reduced by your fault percentage and barred at 51% or more. Whether a helmet affects value depends on the injuries and the facts, and an attorney can push back on inflated fault claims.
to: South Carolina law requires motorcycle operators and passengers under age 21 to wear an approved helmet (S.C. Code § 56-5-3660). State law does not impose that helmet requirement on riders age 21 or older. Whether a helmet question affects the value of a particular claim depends on the injuries and the facts, so have an attorney review yours.
note: FAQ + FAQPage. MC-G1 / B3-G4 resolved, approved 2026-09-30 (Gillin): cut comparative-fault helmet lines to the statute-only wording.
